submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires on the determiner, possessive or quantifier token that directly follows the preposition 'in'/'In' - the token that opens the noun phrase 'in' governs ('in the', 'in a', 'in an', 'in his', 'in their', 'in several'), where peaks run 1.0-3.1 while the same determiners after at/of/on/to/for/with/inside, bare content words after 'in' ('in 1902', 'in Paris', 'in danger'), and ordinary sentence-internal 'the' sit at the ~-0.15 baseline. Strength is graded within that context - highest (~2.3-2.6) when the 'in'-phrase is a comma-set adverbial or parenthetical, near baseline when 'in' is a relational complement of the preceding noun ('a gap in the box', 'a mutation in the gene') - and a sparse, weaker offshoot (~1.0-1.3) also fires on 'been' after 'has/have' and on clause-initial 'It' after a newline.

The harbour town of Ellwood began as little more than a fishing camp in 1843, when a dozen families built wooden huts along the northern shore and dried their catch on racks beside the water. For two decades the settlement grew slowly. Merchants arrived each spring, loaded salt and rope onto carts, and departed before the first autumn gales. Children learned to swim in the cold shallows, and old sailors told stories about ships that had vanished beyond the horizon.

By 1871 the town had a school, two churches, a smithy, and a narrow road that connected the docks with the farms inland. The road flooded every winter, and repairs consumed most of the council's budget. A young engineer named Margaret Ellery proposed a stone embankment, arguing that a protected channel would let larger vessels dock in safety. The council debated the plan for months. Farmers objected to the cost; fishermen worried about the currents; shopkeepers supported anything that brought customers. In the end the vote passed by a single seat.

Construction began in the spring of 1874 and lasted nearly three years. Labourers hauled granite from a quarry six miles away, and masons fitted each block by hand. Storms destroyed part of the work twice, and a fire ruined the timber scaffolding once. Ellery kept a daily journal, recording tides, wages, accidents, and the slow progress of the wall. Her entries reveal a stubborn, practical mind, impatient with ceremony and generous with praise for the crews.

When the embankment opened, the harbour could shelter forty boats at once. Trade doubled over the next decade. A cannery, a chandlery, and a small shipyard appeared along the waterfront, and the population passed three thousand. Visitors from the capital wrote admiring articles about the tidy streets and the handsome lighthouse at the southern tip.

The twentieth century was less kind. The railway bypassed Ellwood in 1908, and the cannery closed during the depression. Young people left for the cities, and the council struggled to maintain services with a shrinking tax base. Even so, the town survived. Retired fishermen repaired their boats, families kept gardens, and the annual regatta continued without interruption.

Restoration efforts began in the 1980s, funded partly by a national heritage grant. Volunteers rebuilt the lighthouse lantern, cleared the old road, and converted the chandlery into a museum. Today the embankment still holds, though engineers inspect it every year, and the harbour remains busy in summer with pleasure craft and small ferries.

The town council recently approved a new plan for the waterfront, and the debate that followed echoed arguments heard a century earlier. Supporters described the proposal as a chance to attract visitors and repair aging docks. Critics warned that the scheme would favour wealthier residents and push working families away from the shore. At a crowded meeting in the old school hall, the mayor promised that any development would respect the character of the town. The final vote, taken after midnight, authorised the council to seek partners and begin a survey of the harbour bed.
